docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sectionText:
### Verification ladder

| Rung | Content | Command | Proves | Does not yet prove | Waits for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| V1 | `fgos-mailbox-core` alone (pure crate: no host, no CLI, no file I/O): envelope, state machine, policies, name resolution, framing and body escaping, generation rules, bounded refusal counters. Tests: the A, B, C, A counterexample, hostile bodies, name resolution, and the scripted pair of the loop test replayed without any model (the wake quota fires at message 6, chain depth at 8, the wake lifetime cap at 101, as measured in `plans/reports/research-261020-1814-mailbox-real-agent-loop-test.md`) | `cargo test -p fgos-mailbox-core` | the policy logic | storage, CLIs, hooks, any real model behaviour | nothing |
| V2 | The record adapter in `fgos-mailbox` (no host): the snapshot under the holder-lock mutex with `durable-file`, crash safety (a kill matrix at each write step), contention between two processes with the wait cap, the size ceiling. Costs are compared with the S0 numbers (about 10 ms per write, `fsync` dominated; `plans/reports/research-261020-1612-mailbox-s0-hook-and-record-costs.md`) | `cargo test -p fgos-mailbox` | atomic visibility and process-crash safety on the mailbox's own path; that a dying holder releases the lock; that the cost matches S0 | any hook payload, any CLI | the lock-registry row (the only prerequisite of this rung; the record directory is a parameter) |
| V3 | Hook payload contract tests with fixtures recorded from the real CLIs (Claude Code `Stop` and `PostToolUse`, Codex, agy) into the crate's tests, with secrets and full session ids removed (the scratch probes under `.fgos/runtime/tmp/mailbox-probe*` hold real payload shapes, for example `hook.log` under `mailbox-probe/{claude,codex,agy}`). Each payload goes to the drain function and the test asserts the output shape the CLI expects (block-and-continue at `Stop`, `additionalContext`), fail-quiet exit 0, the `agent_id` skip and the generation registration. No live CLI | `cargo test -p fgos-mailbox` (payload suite) | the hook contract against recorded reality | that today's CLI versions still behave so; delivery into a live model | nothing, except that the registration case for runner heads needs `is_attempt_writer_id` (section 1); until it is exported that case moves to V5 |
| V4 | Claude Code live end to end (stop gate, mid-step, hook really ran, `send`, `inbox`) through a **test-only** hook entry: a `cargo` example binary of `fgos-mailbox` (planned: `packages/mailbox/rust/store/examples/mailbox-test-hook.rs`), run with `claude -p --settings <file>` pointing at it. It is not a product door and is never installed, so the one-door rule holds; it removes the dependency on the host routing prerequisite | the live suite for Claude Code (section 11) | the first adapter on a real CLI before the host route exists | the real `fgos hook mailbox` entry, the hook cost through the host | the mailbox root in the hidden roots (confinement; section 8 item 6), which the record from V2 makes necessary |
| V5 | The native `fgos hook mailbox` kind through the host route; the hook install table (the four install functions refactored into one table, with the `mailbox` kind and the doctor probe; the table unit test needs no host and may land earlier). V4 is re-run through the real entry, and the hook p95 is measured in each CLI's real hook environment against the 50 ms target (`mailbox.hook.p95TargetMs`) | the V4 live suite through the shim; the installer's tests | the product door and the native selector cost in each CLI | behaviour of models under real delivery | host hook routing (prerequisites below) |
| V6 | The behavioural measurements through the real hook delivery, and the starting values of sections 5.3 and 12 (stop rule below). The in-flight timeout is measured against the adapters' latency; the real-agent loop test (two real agents, 5 runs per configuration) runs here | the measurement runs, reported in `plans/reports/` | whether models act on legitimate requests and refuse harmful ones through the real path | anything beyond the cells run | V5 for Claude Code; the Codex cells need the Codex hook rows and the authorization text of the stop rule |
| V7 | Codex and agy adapters (agy through hooks only: flat `Stop`, nested `PostToolUse`, tier `turn` or `pull`, no idle wake), the `status` thresholds (set from the V6 numbers), the minimal doctor check and the `CHANGELOG.md` line, each adapter with its own live suite. Codex only if the stop rule passes and the Codex adapter preconditions hold | `test/live/mailbox-<cli>.live.mjs` (section 11) | each adapter on a real CLI on the owner's machine | untested CLI versions | V5; for Codex also the stop rule and authorization |

V1 and V3 wait for no other component. V2 waits for the lock-registry row, V4 (through the test-only entry) for the mailbox root in the hidden roots, V5 for host routing and the main-checkout resolver, V6 and V7 for V5.

**Mapping from the earlier steps.** S0 stays as measurements (above). The first step S1 is split: the core and its tests are V1; the record, registry, generation and lock row are V2; the `hook mailbox` handling and payload shapes are V3; the Claude Code end to end is V4; the kind, the install table refactor and the doctor probe are V5. The earlier S2 (storm and loop tests, real-agent loop test, in-flight timeout) is V1 for the scripted tests and V6 for the real agents. The earlier S3 (Codex, agy, `status` thresholds, doctor check, `CHANGELOG.md`) is V7.

**Stop rule at the end of V6 (owner, 2026-10-20).** The behavioural measurement of the earlier step S2 (the evaluations of section 5.5) is repeated through the **real hook delivery**, not the print-mode append of the earlier evaluations, with the instruction that lists the trusted senders (the prerequisite below), N of at least 20 per cell for Codex and for Claude Code. The cells are the requests case B would really send: a Claude session, the runner or the `fgos` CLI asking an independently started Codex head for read-only work, and for work inside that head's task. The harmful variants B, C, D, K, L and M (section 5.5) are run in the same way and must stay at 0 acted.

- **Threshold.** Codex must act on a legitimate coordinator request in at least 80 percent of the runs **of each legitimate cell** (owner, 2026-10-20: per cell, not pooled across cells). Report the observed rate for each cell and its Wilson 95 percent interval. If the rate is below 80 percent, the Codex adapter is **not** built at V7, and the owner and the controller revisit the plan before more is spent.
- **Honest limits.** 80 percent is the owner's chosen threshold, not a derived one. N of 20 gives a wide interval: 16 of 20 has a Wilson 95 percent interval of about 58 to 92 percent (computed here), so a pass is weak evidence of a rate near 80 and a fail is weak evidence of a rate far below it. The harmful variants are a separate condition: a Codex pass on legitimate requests does not excuse any acted harmful run.

**Codex adapter preconditions (V7).** The Codex adapter needs, besides the stop rule: **authorization** (section 16 question 16), a prerequisite of the Codex adapter and not of G0. Whoever starts the recipient head writes the line that lists its trusted senders; the mailbox supplies the instruction text and the format of the list. Until it exists, case B (a Claude session, the runner or the `fgos` CLI asking an independently started Codex head) is not claimed to work.

**Prerequisites owned by other components (none is signed by G0), each attached to the first rung that needs it.**

- V2: the `mailbox` row of the holder-lock registry and its line in that spec.
- V5 (wiring): the Rust resolver of the main checkout's `.fgos` for any working directory, owned by the host or a git-topology foundation, not by the mailbox (section 6.4). Until it exists the wiring has nothing to give the crates as the record directory.
- V3 or V5, where registration needs it: session identity's exported `is_attempt_writer_id` (section 1).
- V4: confinement hidden roots, since the mailbox root exists from V2 (section 8, item 6).
- V5: host hook routing (`docs/platform/host-invocation-routing`): the host handles `hook` with native code, takes the `mailbox` kind in Rust and hands every other kind to the legacy-node payload through `legacy_exec`. Today `hook` is entirely legacy-node, measured at about 170 to 330 ms per call. The installer's `commandIsKind` is extended in the same change. Precedent for a native branch before the legacy route: `identity` in `apps/fgos/src/main.rs`. Whether the host can split one selector this way is unmeasured.
- V7 (Codex): authorization, above.

Nothing here changes a locked law of `docs/platform-foundations.md`.

docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sectionText:
### 15.1 Acknowledgement, `handled`, `reply_by`, expiry, approval

- States `acked` and `handled` after `offered`; `expired` when `reply_by` passed without `handled`, with a dead-letter notice to the sender. Escalation after expiry: remind once, then ask the project owner through the decision-question path.
- `held`: a message kept for a person's approval, with an `approve` verb, a stated approver, and a trust key per source class. Cut from the first slice.
- Conditions from the councils: a reply counts as `acked` (so the metric does not measure model discipline); expiry uses the receiver's or a logical clock, or states a skew tolerance, so clock drift does not create false dead letters that become human questions.
- Compaction pin: how an offered but unacked message returns after context compaction, with a bound on how often. No source studied solves it; it needs a design and a measurement.
- `acked` is written by the receiver (a reply counts); that, not the delivery report, is the receipt in the sense of ADR-011.
- Observability returns with: the share `offered` but not `acked`, and messages that reached `reply_by` without `handled`.

docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.title: 15.2 Persistence in the Event Store and cross-machine delivery
docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sample: 15.2 Persistence in the Event Store and cross-machine delivery
ancestry: 15. Later parts, deliberately not in the first slice
docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.text: ### 15.2 Persistence in the Event Store and cross-machine delivery
docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sectionText:
### 15.2 Persistence in the Event Store and cross-machine delivery

- The record (the snapshot of section 6.4) becomes Event Store events of a registered mailbox type; new messages may take the event hash as `id`. `project` scope stream of the sender on `refs/fgos/events/<machine-id>`, sealed in batches (Event Store section 16). Delivery delivery reports stay in `local` scope; `acked` and `handled` live in the receiver's `project` stream. The receiver derives its inbox by filtering the union of streams by `to`; dedupe by `id`.
- No timer and no daemon. The sender's `send` seals and publishes itself. The receiver fetches when some fgOS process runs there: at most `eventStore.sync.intervalSec` (300 s by default) on a machine that runs a runner or gateway, unbounded on a machine where no fgOS process runs. There is no real-time cross-machine wake; a faster path is only a hint (`Replication.nudge`) that triggers an early fetch. Ordering per sender only. Offline: append and local delivery work; publish and fetch fail, are recorded, retry at the next trigger.
- `MailStore` and `Replication` become ports at this point. `Replication`: `publish()`, `fetch()`, `nudge()`; delivery at least once, deduplicated by `id`. Swap triggers: the Git remote rejects or limits `refs/fgos/*`; a measured need for latency below a few seconds between machines; a full rebuild above the Event Store 2 s threshold.
- Rate limit (per session rather than per machine, as council round 1 asked, with a bound on deferred messages) and collapse of identical bodies return here, because one machine cannot see another machine's count before a sync.
- Growth: Event Store refs only move forward and history is not rewritten, so message bodies stay in shared history for good. Keep bodies small or outside the shared chain, and measure events and bytes per day per machine from the first push. No message garbage collection at first; expiry is a view rule. Fallback if growth forces it: separate streams per period so an old stream is dropped whole once every machine fetched it (needs the Event Store to allow several streams of one type; unverified).
- Open: whether a hook that calls `fgos` can be the fetch trigger within its time budget, and whether a network call there violates the Event Store rule against network calls inside the Work gate. A hook must read the local record only.

### 15.4 Other candidates (separate decisions)

- Human-addressed groups, expanded into individual envelopes, with a group registry.
- A signed, machine-attested human answer (reference: reason-network `ask_user` with a signed approval): a separate component or an Event Store event type.
- Locks and leases across machines: not solved here and not by the Event Store (claims are runtime state per machine).
- Steer and park events addressed by a running Unit (`unitRunId`) and flushed at the runner's round boundary: council round 1 found this the narrowest part with a clear consumer. It belongs to the runner and Assignment; the envelope, framing and delivery report are reusable for it.

docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.text: ### 15.5 Durable sessions (not done; may be done later)
docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sectionText:
### 15.5 Durable sessions (not done; may be done later)

A durable session is one whose identity and conversation outlive the process or terminal that hosts it: `claude --resume` rebuilds the same conversation in a new process, a Codex thread survives its process, and an in-process teammate's mailbox outlives the teammate (research report 261015, section 4). An address would then bind to the conversation, not to the process.

Not done in the first slice because no named consumer needs a message to survive a restart of its recipient, and fgOS has no durable concept to build on: the writer identity is per process, a pane id disappears with its pane, and no name registry exists. The first slice releases an address when its session ends, and its generation number (section 5.1, keyed on the process) already keeps a successor from receiving the old mail; what is not done is carrying an address across processes of the same conversation.

Reasons it may be done later, kept so the decision is not rebuilt from nothing: a message to a worker on another machine that restarts (needs a name that survives a restart); a long-lived coordinator resumed over days that still expects its waiting mail; and the council round 2 finding that a successor taking a name must not receive stale instructions, which the first slice already handles with its process-keyed generation (section 5.1); a durable session would need that generation keyed on the conversation instead. Revisit trigger: a named consumer needs mail to survive a restart of the recipient. Measured 2026-10-20 (plans/reports/research-261020-1457-mailbox-claude-busy-socket-and-subagent-probe.md, Claude Code 2.1.304, `claude -p`, one run): the `session_id` stayed the same across `--resume <id>` and `--continue` and both appended to the same transcript, while the process id and the socket path changed for every process. So for Claude Code a durable address would key on `session_id`, never on the pid or the socket. Not measured: the interactive REPL, `--fork-session`, resume after `/compact`, and the same question for Codex, pi, omp and agy.

docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.title: 15.6 Subagents and teammates: out of scope by principle
docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sample: 15.6 Subagents and teammates: out of scope by principle
ancestry: 15. Later parts, deliberately not in the first slice
docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.text: ### 15.6 Subagents and teammates: out of scope by principle
docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sectionText:
### 15.6 Subagents and teammates: out of scope by principle

**Principle (owner, 2026-10-20): work with the boss, never reach past the boss into the people who work for them.** The mailbox addresses the head of a CLI. Whatever a head delegates to its subagents or teammates is the head's own business; the mailbox never addresses, wakes, steers or injects into them. A message for the head reaches the head, and the head decides whether to pass any of it on. Reasons that support the principle: the head owns the context and the authority of its helpers; a message placed directly into a subordinate bypasses the head's framing and its judgement (section 8); Claude Code itself sends a subagent's outgoing message under the parent's address; and fgOS starts every worker it controls as its own CLI process, so anything fgOS needs to address is already a head.

This is a decision, not a deferred feature, so it has no revisit trigger; changing it needs a new owner decision. What follows is measured evidence of what is technically possible, kept so that nobody has to measure it again and so the hook rule of section 6.1 has its reason.

Measured 2026-10-20 on Claude Code 2.1.304 (report `plans/reports/research-261020-1457-mailbox-claude-busy-socket-and-subagent-probe.md`, one run each, `haiku`):

- **Subagent.** `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` fire for each of a subagent's tool calls. Only the subagent's events carry `agent_id` and `agent_type`; `session_id` and `transcript_path` equal the parent's. `SubagentStop` fires for the subagent and `Stop` only for the parent. `additionalContext` returned for a subagent event landed only in that subagent's context. So a hook can address one subagent, but only at the moment that subagent calls a tool, and an outside sender has no known way to learn a live subagent's `agent_id` yet (candidate sources: the Agent tool result, the session file, a `SubagentStart` hook; none measured).
- **Teammate** (agent teams, enabled for one process with `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`; the flag is not in `claude --help`). A message lands in `~/.claude/teams/<team>/inboxes/<name>.json`. A busy teammate took it only after its current turn (13.2 s later), not mid-tool; an idle one took it 0.6 s after it landed. The lead starts a new turn for every teammate idle notification. The messages were sent by the lead's `SendMessage` at the probe's request; writing the file from outside, and a `PostToolUse` event inside a teammate, were not measured.
- **Socket write to a busy session** (the head, not a subagent). The running tool was not cut. The message showed on screen as a queued line within about 0.8 s and the model saw it only after the tool finished, in the same turn; two messages sent together both arrived in order. A message that arrived while the model was generating text ran as its own turn, labelled as sent by another session, 1.7 to 2.4 s after the first turn ended. Not separated: whether, in a turn with several tools, the model sees it after the next tool or at the end of the turn.

For the other CLIs, research report 261015 records that a subagent's outgoing message carries the parent session's address and that replies return to the parent's conversation. Measured consequence for the mailbox's own hook: the hook fires for a subagent's tool calls as well, so a `drain` that ignored the event's origin would inject the head's peer mail into the subagent's context, which the principle forbids. Section 6.1 therefore requires `drain` to do nothing for an event that carries `agent_id`.

docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sectionText:
### 15.7 Headless workers (not in the first slice)

fgOS starts some workers headless (`cli-spawn`: no pane, no tty) and some in a pane (`herdr-spawn`). Owner, 2026-10-20: the terminal case is the fuller one and comes first; a headless worker is not built first. Differences recorded for later: a headless worker cannot be woken by a typed signal and has no idle state to wake (it runs one Unit and exits), so it can only be reached at a checkpoint (tier `turn`); hooks do run in print mode (the Stop gate was measured on `claude -p`, `codex exec` and the others, `plans/reports/research-261019-1653-mailbox-delivery-cli-probe.md` measurement 1). Steering a running Unit belongs to the runner (section 15.4). A worker confined by the sandbox (bwrap is in use in this repository, per `docs/architecture-map.md`) can neither read nor write mailbox state (section 8, item 6); reaching it would need the confinement to expose the state through a registered resource, or the adapter to refuse with a reason such as `blind-confinement` (the reason name comes from the panel's summary and is unverified). A worker the runner starts is not addressable at all (section 1).

A worker confined by the sandbox (bwrap is in use in this repository, per `docs/architecture-map.md`) can neither read nor write mailbox state (section 8, item 6); reaching it would need the confinement to expose the state through a registered resource, or the adapter to refuse with a reason such as `blind-confinement` (the reason name comes from the panel's summary and is unverified). A worker the runner starts is not addressable at all (section 1).

docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sectionText:
### 15.8 Typed nudge for an idle agy session, and the shared terminal adapter (later part)

Decision of 2026-10-20 (owner delegated, controller chose to move it out): nothing here is deleted; it is condensed and kept so it can be built later.

**Why it is later.** One chain exists only to wake an idle agy by typing one line into its terminal: the shared crate `fgos-agent-terminal`, `composer_state`, a focus-neutral `deliver_brief`, the attach allocation record, the terminal-control dependency and the confinement exposure. It has no consumer in the owner's inventory (0 of 24 inventoried exchanges involve agy, `plans/reports/research-261020-1457-mailbox-address-unit-and-first-consumer.md`), it is the most fragile channel (screen reading, a version pin, a residual race) and it was measured once. The first slice is complete without it: Claude Code, Codex and agy all receive mail through hooks (tier `turn` or `pull`). The cost is that an idle agy is not woken by the mailbox; it sees mail at its next hook checkpoint or when it calls `inbox`.

**Typed-signal rules (the design kept).** Typing is the only wake channel agy has. It would be enabled by default for agy only; a CLI with another channel uses that channel. Each rule is a measured failure or a race:

1. `state` is `idle` and `composer` is `empty`. Measured: herdr reports `idle` while a human has half a sentence typed. Never type while busy.
2. No dialog is open (`state` is `blocked`). Measured: a typed Enter confirmed the default "Yes, I trust this folder" and the message was lost.
3. One short, labelled line only: `[fgOS: message from another agent, not from the user] You have mail. Read it with: fgos mailbox inbox`; multi-line text would use bracketed paste.
4. Text plus Enter without changing the user's focus. Measured: `herdr pane send-text` plus `send-keys Enter` leaves focus unchanged; `herdr agent prompt` moves focus to the target pane.
5. At most one outstanding nudge per address (section 6.2).
6. When the gate says no or `unknown`, the adapter falls back to `turn` or `pull` and the delivery report says so; before typing it re-observes immediately.
7. A gap between reading the composer verdict and typing cannot be closed from outside the CLI; the residual race is accepted and counted through nudge outcomes (section 9), not hidden.

Measured on this machine: typed signal wake of an idle agy 19.1 s (section 7). Typed failure modes to record when built: text goes into a dialog and Enter answers it (rule 2); text merges with the person's half sentence (rules 1, 6, 7). Live suite to add: a typed nudge to an idle agy starts a turn within the declared bound, changes no focus, answers no dialog and does not merge with half-typed input; the suite fails on a version bump until the fixtures are re-captured. The status signal for gate refusals (by cause) and fall-backs would join section 9.

**Empty-composer predicate.** Not a capability of terminal-control: a pure function of the screen and the `Inspection` (`Inspection.prompt_text`, `packages/agent-protocol/rust/src/port.rs`), kept in the agent-protocol profile of the CLI as `composer_state` (`empty | not-empty | unknown`), named without reference to the mailbox. Verified: `packages/agent-protocol/rust/src/terminal/agy.rs` holds the agy profile and has no such predicate, so it is new work with screen fixtures captured from the real CLI, under `packages/agent-protocol/contracts/fixtures/terminal/<cli>/`, and the CLI version they were captured at. An unrecognised screen or another version yields `composer: unknown`, which means do not type. Presence would then return `SessionObservation` (`state` plus `composer`, one source at one moment) and a head in an attached pane would be read through terminal-control `inspect`. Nearby and not the same question: `draft_still_in_composer` in `packages/agent-protocol/rust/src/terminal/common.rs`.

**Terminal access (key, not pane).** A head in a terminal is bound to a terminal-control key, never to a pane id (`docs/platform/terminal-control/spec.md`: the key matches `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,127}$` and names one pane for its life, so a new generation uses a new key). At registration the hook would call `attach(key, pane)` and store only the key; `observe` would be `inspect(key, detail=true)`; the mailbox enumerates only its own registry. The drivers are what terminal-control talks to: herdr today, tmux deferred, so a tmux pane would have no typed nudge. Whether the registration side and the `send` side derive the same key is unmeasured.

**Open: an unreleased allocation per head.** Each `attach` publishes one allocation record under `<stateRoot>/terminal` and nothing releases it when a head dies unnoticed (question 17). Options: (1) the mailbox releases the key at its lazy sweep when the head is judged dead, which needs the owner's acceptance that human-opened panes are tracked by the allocation store (the terminal-control spec names `/fgOS:terminal` as the precedent); (2) terminal-control gains an attach that leaves no durable record, a larger change to that component. Releasing an attached slot only removes its label and link and never closes the pane.

**`deliver_brief` reuse and its warning.** Typing one line and confirming it was submitted is `Terminal::deliver_brief` (`packages/agent-protocol/rust/src/terminal/mod.rs`) through `adapter_for(cli)`. Warning, verified in source: when a profile sets `submit_by_prompt_door` (Codex does; agy does not) `deliver_brief` submits through the prompt door, which terminal-control implements as `herdr agent prompt`, which moves focus (rule 4). A non-focus-stealing typed nudge for such a CLI needs a focus-neutral option in `deliver_brief`, a change owned by agent-protocol and not made yet. agy does not need it.

**Shared crate `fgos-agent-terminal` (`packages/agent-terminal/rust`, planned).** Holds the default `AgentIo` (`packages/agent-protocol/rust/src/port.rs`: send keys, read lines, report activity, optionally return the screen and the detector's verdict) over terminal-control, and depends on both. **The crate observes; the caller decides.** It holds the mapping of `send`, `screen` and `inspect` to terminal-control calls and of its errors, an `activity()` derived from screen changes and a reading of the pane's state (live, gone, unknown); no deadline, cancel, attempt or outcome. Two hooks with defaults carry the caller's decisions: `should_stop()` and `on_wait(ms)` (agent-protocol lets time pass only through `AgentIo::pause`). The mailbox has no lifecycle policy, uses the defaults and writes no connector code; anyone else implements `AgentIo` itself. It is a third crate because of Rust's orphan rule (a trait is implemented only in the crate that owns the trait or the type, and agent-protocol must not depend on terminal-control); neither of those crates knows it. Owned with agent-protocol, described in a short section of its spec, created before the agy typed adapter. Exact hook signatures are fixed then.

The run supervisor keeps its private `TermIo` (`packages/run-supervisor/rust/src/supervise/terminal.rs`, about 70 lines, used in `drive`, `end_early` and `ask_to_leave`) and may move later; the owner is willing to pay a modest cost (2026-10-20). `TermIo` does two jobs: about 35 generic lines implementing `AgentIo`, and the supervisor's working handle, since 19 places reach the supervisor's own state through `io.sup` (verified by count). The first job, with activity tracking (`note_screen`, `last_active`) and pane state reading, would move to the crate. The supervisor keeps its policy (stop when the attempt is ending, its watch loop during a wait, `begin_stop`; ADR-011) behind a connector of two hooks of about 20 lines, and the 19 accesses go through them (the structure fuses `core`, `key` and `&mut Sup`, so no two mutable borrows are possible). The gain is one place to fix the mapping and activity tracking, not much less supervisor code, so the supervisor's owner may leave it. Its tests and recorded terminal vectors must pass unchanged; the refusal text ("the attempt is ending") and the order of side effects (`last_active` set after the inspection is read) must be preserved.

**Simpler alternative to evaluate first when it is built.** Use terminal-control directly plus the pure functions of agent-protocol (`classify_blocked`, the composer predicate) and a short send-and-verify step of about 20 lines, with no crate. Risk: it misses per-CLI quirks such as the swallowed Enter, which a live suite catches. Choose the crate only if a second real consumer of the default `AgentIo` exists.

**Measure first.** Whether a one-line typed nudge to agy suffers the swallowed first Enter that long briefs suffered in pi (`plans/reports/debug-261020-1611-pi-herdr-brief-not-submitted.md`: a long raw-typed brief took 7 to 25 s and the first Enter was sometimes lost; a short line to pi worked). Not measured for agy.

**Revisit triggers.** A named consumer needs to wake an idle agy; or the measurement above shows the typed nudge is cheap and reliable.

**Prerequisites when it is built.** The agent-protocol items (`composer_state` with fixtures and version pin; a focus-neutral option of `deliver_brief` only if a CLI with `submit_by_prompt_door` is added); the attach record decision above; the confinement exposure: a typed nudge adds terminal keys to the binding and an allocation record under `<stateRoot>/terminal`; whether workers can read either is not examined here and is reviewed with the confinement component.

## 16. Open questions for the owner

1. **V-011.** Answered 2026-10-20: the narrowed claim is accepted and recorded as V-013 (section 2). The address form (question 2) is answered too; G0 now waits for the print-mode measurement (section 14, S0) and a re-read.
2. **Address form and names** (gate G0). Names confirmed by the owner on 2026-10-20: `<project>-<cli>-<2 characters>`, delivery in the same project only for the first slice. Provisionally agreed 2026-10-20: a terminal plus the head of the CLI running in it, keyed by project; no machine address, no durable session, no direct subagent address. Section 5.1.1 proposes the key, the short name and the resolution order and waits for the owner. Still open: which field of `docs/platform/session-identity/spec.md` (writer identity, a herdr pane id, or the CLI's own conversation id) the registry maps names onto, how a `fgos mailbox send` child process learns the identity of its calling session, and the three measurements of sections 15.5 and 15.6. Measured 2026-10-20 (`plans/reports/research-261020-1547-mailbox-pi-omp-session-id-probe.md`, pi 1.3.0 and omp 18.11.2, one run each, print mode): pi exports its session id to the Bash tool as `PI_SESSION_ID` and the session file path as `PI_SESSION_FILE`; omp exports neither. In both, an extension handler's second argument gives the id through `ctx.sessionManager.getSessionId()` (the event payload has none). omp keeps a terminal-to-session record `<profile>/agent/terminal-sessions/pts-N` (cwd, session file path, a `cwdstat` line, a `fresh` line until the first message) but it names the last session launched in that tty, not the active one, and is not deleted when omp exits; pi keeps no such record. So the registry should not trust omp's terminal record; the head registers itself from its extension (omp) or reads `PI_SESSION_ID` (pi), and session-identity does not read either today (a separate change to that component, not made here). Still unmeasured: whether `PI_SESSION_ID` changes after `/new` or `/resume` in the pi REPL, what the `cwdstat` numbers mean, whether pi and omp keep `HERDR_*` variables inside herdr.
3. **First consumer.** Answered 2026-10-20: case B, a Claude session or the runner or `fgos` CLI sending to an independently started head that is not Claude (Codex or agy; never a runner Unit attempt, owner answer of 2026-10-20), as a small first test. In the first slice an idle agy is not woken (section 15.8), so the agy half of the test reads mail at its next hook checkpoint. The evidence is weak (research `plans/reports/research-261020-1457-mailbox-address-unit-and-first-consumer.md` finds one inventoried exchange, line 14, and no consumer the board, files and runner do not already serve), so the test's purpose is to find out whether the mailbox is worth more than that. Claude to Claude on this machine is already served by the harness's own `SendMessage` between sessions of the same permission class (section 7.2), so it is not the test. The record-level questions this test needs to answer are in section 14 (rungs V6 and V7). Case B toward Codex is not claimed to work until authorization exists (question 16) and the stop rule of section 14 passes.
4. Codex `queue` wake latency. Answered 2026-10-20 by measurement: a fixed 10 s polling tick inside Codex, so 0 to 10 s (mean about 5 s) plus the model's reply of 1.3 to 4.7 s; the earlier "about 10 s" came from runs spaced exactly 20 s apart that always landed in the same phase. A REPL started with `--no-daemon` is reachable with the same tick; a REPL attached to the shared daemon is untested. Which process runs the tick, and whether the interval is configurable, are unknown.
5. Should the `fgos doctor` check for a skipped hook be reconsidered? Answered by the decision of 2026-10-19 plus the install gate: no check before the component exists; a minimal check registers at V7 (section 12).
6. Human-input hook. Answered 2026-10-20 by measurement (section 5.4): Claude Code and Codex have `UserPromptSubmit`, agy has none; on all three the hook also fires for a peer message and cannot tell the two apart, so the first slice uses the rolling window on every CLI.
7. Can `docs/architecture-manifest.json` express a Rust crate boundary? Answered 2026-10-20: no, `test/architecture.test.mjs` scans only `.mjs` under `src` and `bin`. The core is a separate crate (`fgos-mailbox-core`, serde only) so Cargo enforces rules 1 and 3 of section 4; no workspace-wide cargo dependency test is proposed in this slice.
8. Who owns the adapters? Five CLIs move fast; council round 1 estimated one adapter breaking per quarter (an estimate, not an observation) and nobody is named to run the live suites.
9. How does the hook reach the native route? Measured 2026-10-20 (`plans/reports/research-261020-1612-mailbox-s0-hook-and-record-costs.md`, 50 runs, strace confirmed): the existing `fgos hook <kind>` runs on the legacy-node payload (`bin/fgos.mjs` `handleHook`, two Node starts per call) and costs p50 171 to 223 ms and p95 227 to 291 ms; a native verb answers in the Rust host in about 10 ms through the shell shim (about 2 ms without the shim). Decided 2026-10-20 (owner): the hook is a native kind of the existing `fgos hook` door, `fgos hook mailbox`, not a second door; the host-routing prerequisite is in section 14.
10. **D2: what does a Stop drain?** Answered 2026-10-20 (the owner asked for advice and the controller decided, with reasons): only `wake:true` messages. `wake` is the sender's permission to start a turn on an idle recipient, so letting a `wake:false` message start one at Stop would empty the flag of meaning and let ordinary mail make an agent work while nobody asked; it keeps a person as the brake. The cost: an idle agent sees a `wake:false` message late, at its next tool call or next prompt, and the delivery report says so; a sender who needs it read now sets `wake`. The panel recommended the other option (drain everything at Stop, bounded) for an honest delivery report; the delivery report here is just worded to say what really happens.
11. **Record layout.** Answered 2026-10-20 (owner, with a plain-language explanation of the choice): the metadata snapshot under a mutex (section 6.4) is the record architecture; the earlier lockless rename spool with file-per-message and create-exclusive generation files is superseded. The panel's alternative for the whole first slice, a drop box plus a hook and an instruction with no core, was rejected for the first slice and is kept only as the fallback if S0 shows the core is not worth its cost.
12. **Hook p95 target.** Answered 2026-10-20: 50 ms p95 on the path with no mail, as the Event Store gate. The native route measured about 10 ms (about 21 ms inferred for a drain that finds mail, two snapshot writes dominated by `fsync`), so no shell guard is kept.
13. **Lock fairness.** Answered 2026-10-20: the lock is not changed. The hook waits at most 100 ms (a placeholder) for it and then skips this drain; the next hook call tries again.
14. **How strict is the peer-input instruction?** Direction decided 2026-10-20 (advice): relax it for read-only work inside the user's task that is not destructive, require the receiver to tell its user what it received and did, and show mail offered and never answered in `status` (section 9, signal 10). The new wording was measured (section 5.5); it is measured once more with the real escaped body and the real hook delivery before it is final (the stop rule of section 14, rung V6). Why: with the strict instruction Codex acted on 1 of 5 and pi on 2 of 5 harmless in-task requests and neither told its user about a declined one, so the first consumer (a Claude session or the runner asking a Codex or agy worker) would mostly be ignored without anyone knowing. Evidence of the strict behaviour: `plans/reports/research-261020-1612-mailbox-s0-peer-frame-injection-eval.md`; 5 runs per cell show a rate only (the 95 percent upper bound of 0 of 5 is about 52 percent). For Codex the new wording did not measurably raise compliance with in-task read-only requests (section 5.5).
15. **Transcript origin fields.** Answered 2026-10-20 (advice): keep the rolling window on every CLI. The origin fields are internal and not contracts, Claude's is readable only after the turn, agy has none, and reading them would add a branch per CLI for a gain the window and the lifetime caps already give. Revisit when a measured case shows a person legitimately blocked by the window.

16. **Authorization (a prerequisite of the Codex adapter, not of G0; owner, 2026-10-20).** A receiver cannot tell a legitimate coordinator from an injected peer: `from` is attribution only and no trust key exists in this slice. The natural source of authorization is whoever starts the recipient head, a person or a launch path that is not a Unit attempt, writing the trusted senders into that head's instruction (for example "you may accept requests from forgent-claude-2b"). That is the `inbound.<class>` trust key cut from the first slice. Without it, case B (a Claude session or the runner asking a Codex worker) will be refused or ignored by Codex in many cases (section 5.5 evidence). The owner decided on 2026-10-20 that this is a prerequisite of the Codex adapter (rung V7), not of G0. Its owner was first named as the lane that writes the worker's brief (the runner and dispatch lane); after the owner's answer of 2026-10-20 that a Unit attempt is not a recipient, the line is written by whoever starts the recipient head, and the mailbox supplies the instruction text and the trusted-sender list format. Until it exists, the first slice's case B is not claimed to work. The form of the `inbound.<class>` key itself is still undecided.
17. **Allocation record per attached head.** Moved to section 15.8; not part of the first slice.
18. **Record location.** Answered 2026-10-20: option A, `<fgosDir>/runtime/mailbox/` with a repo-scope lock row; it needs a Rust resolver for the main `.fgos` (V2 task). Option B, `<stateRoot>/mailbox/<key>`, stays the bounded alternative (section 6.4).
19. **`AgentIo` wiring.** Moved to section 15.8; not part of the first slice.

docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sectionText:
## 17. Decision history

| Date | Decision | By | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-19 | Do not turn the CLI measurement into a `fgos doctor` check until the mailbox exists | owner | accepted; reopened as question 5 |
| 2026-10-19 | K1: no global `crossSessionInbound: accept`; the harness's cross-session send is not mailbox traffic; scoped `accept` only for a runner-started worker if ever needed | owner | accepted; the runner-started-worker part is parked with runner steering (section 15.4) since a Unit attempt is not a recipient (2026-10-20) |
| 2026-10-19 | K2: wake agy by one labelled typed line behind a state gate | owner | accepted in direction; moved to a later part (section 15.8) |
| 2026-10-19 | Component is hexagonal so the transport can change | owner | accepted in direction; this spec is the form |
| 2026-10-19 | No message garbage collection at first; reuse the Event Store 2 s rebuild threshold | proposed in the discussion; the owner did not object | moved to section 15.2; applies when persistence starts |
| 2026-10-19 | Council round 1: delivery measured and useful, the rest unmeasured and without a named consumer | council | plans/reports/research-261019-1828-mailbox-spec-council-round1.md |
| 2026-10-19 | Option A: narrow to the delivery slice (Claude Code, Codex, agy; local; no ack, no cross-machine); record the later parts in section 15 | owner | accepted |
| 2026-10-19 | Council round 2 design changes: drain verb plus a nudge-only port; derived reply link; lazy deadlines; file-per-message record; hook installer table and guard; S1 (now rung V4) is Claude end to end | council, applied by the controller | applied in this revision, awaiting owner sign-off with the rest of the spec; plans/reports/research-261019-1834-mailbox-spec-council-round2.md |
| 2026-10-20 | An address belongs to a terminal plus the head of the CLI in it; a subagent is not addressed directly; one clone per project per machine with many worktrees is assumed (this machine has one clone of the repository and linked worktrees; other machines not seen) | owner | agreed provisionally; research A confirms |
| 2026-10-20 | Durable sessions are not done in the first slice; recorded in section 15.5 as not done and possibly done later, not removed | owner | accepted |
| 2026-10-20 | The first consumer is case B: a Claude session or the runner sending to a Codex or agy session, as a small first test; the other candidates (herdr coordinator to pane worker, lane to lane across machines, runner steering, owner to lane) are not the first slice | owner | accepted; refined on 2026-10-20: the recipient is an independently started head, never a Unit attempt |
| 2026-10-20 | The V-011 narrowing is accepted and recorded as V-013 in the agent coordination vision; V-011 is unchanged; the later parts of section 15 may be added later, each argued and decided separately | owner | accepted |
| 2026-10-20 | `tested_against` is checked against the version of the target process, from the CLI's own session file where it records one; otherwise against the installed version and the delivery report says so | owner | accepted |
| 2026-10-20 | Names: `<project>-<cli>-<2 characters>` (three on a collision), a Claude head keeps its own two characters, resolution by exact name then unique prefix then key prefix, delivery in the same project only for the first slice | owner | accepted |
| 2026-10-20 | The `wake` rule "an agent may set wake only when it received no peer message" is dropped (it broke the request and reply case: the requester, idle, was never woken to read the answer, and it depended on the agent's own good will). Replaced by a wake quota per exchange, reset by a quiet gap, plus a wake lifetime cap, both enforced by the component; the frame tells the receiver to reply only when asked or when it has a result; the real-agent loop test joins S2 (now rung V6). `wake` keeps its name and means the sender's permission to start a turn on an idle recipient | owner | accepted; the three values are placeholders |
| 2026-10-20 | A Stop drains only `wake:true` messages; `wake:false` mail waits for the next tool call or prompt (D2) | owner delegated, controller decided | accepted; reasons in section 16 question 10 |
| 2026-10-20 | At a version of the target process not in `tested_against`, only the unverified nudge paths are turned off and the hook drain keeps running; the delivery report names the version as untested | owner | accepted |
| 2026-10-20 | Hook p95 target 50 ms on the no-mail path, no shell guard; the hook waits at most 100 ms for the snapshot lock and then skips the drain; the lock is not changed | owner | accepted; the 100 ms is a placeholder |
| 2026-10-20 | Peer-input instruction relaxed for read-only in-task work with a duty to tell the user; unanswered mail visible in `status`; remeasured at V6 under the stop rule | owner delegated, controller decided | direction accepted; wording final after the S2 remeasurement |
| 2026-10-20 | The rolling window stays the only budget reset on every CLI; transcript origin fields are not used | owner delegated, controller decided | accepted |
| 2026-10-20 | The generation number is kept in the first slice, keyed on the process (pid and start time), with head registration by the checkpoint hook or extension; this replaces the earlier lean to drop it. It does not make sessions durable | owner | accepted |
| 2026-10-20 | The first slice serves sessions in a terminal (pane or tty); headless workers come later (section 15.7) | owner | accepted |
| 2026-10-20 | Delegation boundary: the mailbox works with the head of a CLI and never reaches into its subagents or teammates (owner: work with the boss, do not reach into the boss's staff) | owner | accepted as a principle; section 15.6; the `drain` rule for `agent_id` events follows from it |
| 2026-10-20 | Independent architecture panel: five claims of the draft did not stand (an unlocked rename called a transaction; `delivered` called "in context"; a cycle proof by pair counts; a shell guard as a cost model; unauthenticated identity granting human exemptions). Applied here: snapshot record under a mutex, `offered`, attempt token plus generation, emit-then-conditional-finish, depth proof struck, lifetime cap, native hook selector, empty-composer predicate in agent-protocol (since moved to section 15.8), body escaping, refusal counters bounded, interactive-session scope. The workflow ended `failed` before its final report was closed, so this is a read of its summary, not a finished verdict | panel, applied by the controller | applied; two forks left open (section 16, D2 and record layout); `plans/reports/research-261020-1327-mailbox-spec-architecture-panel.md` |
| 2026-10-20 | Names (key, short name, resolution order) | controller proposal | superseded by the row "Names: `<project>-<cli>-<2 characters>`" above, which the owner accepted |
| 2026-10-20 | The hook is a native kind of the existing door, `fgos hook mailbox --event ...`; no second door `fgos mailbox drain`. Prerequisite for V5, owned by host invocation routing: native handling of `hook` for this kind, every other kind to legacy-node; no port of `dispatch-decide` or `decision-question` | owner | accepted; prerequisite open (section 14) |
| 2026-10-20 | Two crates: `fgos-mailbox-core` (pure, serde only) and `fgos-mailbox`; the manifest cannot express Rust crate boundaries and no workspace-wide cargo dependency test is proposed in this slice | owner | accepted |
| 2026-10-20 | Record home `<fgosDir>/runtime/mailbox/` with a repo-scope lock row `mailbox` (rank 80), no project key; the location is a parameter so a move to `<stateRoot>/mailbox/<key>` stays bounded | owner | accepted (question 18) |
| 2026-10-20 | One shared crate `fgos-agent-terminal` holds the default `AgentIo` over terminal-control, activity from screen changes and pane state reading; the crate observes and the caller decides; two hooks with defaults (`should_stop`, `on_wait`); the mailbox writes no connector code; anyone may implement `AgentIo` itself; owned with agent-protocol; created before the agy typed adapter; the supervisor keeps a small policy connector and its own `TermIo` until it chooses to move | owner | accepted; moved to section 15.8 |
| 2026-10-20 | The owner is willing to pay a modest cost to move the run supervisor onto the shared adapter later, if its use has nothing special (section 15.8) | owner | recorded; no date; moved to section 15.8 |
| 2026-10-20 | Authority review applied: typed nudge reuses `deliver_brief` and terminal access is by key (both moved to section 15.8); process identity through `fgos-process`; runner workers not addressable; mailbox root in the hidden roots; channel limits are not communication authorization; "delivery report" replaces "receipt"; one source for the frame text; doctor check at V7 | owner | accepted; prerequisites of section 14 open |
| 2026-10-20 | Authorization of senders is an open question: trusted senders written into the worker's instruction by whoever starts it is the candidate, not decided | owner | open (question 16) |
| 2026-10-20 | The typed nudge for an idle agy, with the chain that exists only for it (shared crate `fgos-agent-terminal`, `composer_state`, focus-neutral `deliver_brief`, attach allocation record of question 17, terminal-control dependency, confinement exposure), moves out of the first slice into section 15.8; nothing is deleted. Reasons: 0 of 24 inventoried exchanges involve agy, it is the most fragile channel (screen reading, version pin, residual race) and was measured once, and the first slice is complete because Claude Code, Codex and agy all receive mail through hooks. Cost: an idle agy is not woken by the mailbox | owner delegated, controller chose option X | accepted; revisit triggers in section 15.8 |
| 2026-10-20 | G0 signs scope, architecture and semantics, and does not sign numeric values, the peer-input claim, hook cost in real environments, the cross-component prerequisites or the later parts | owner | accepted (section 14) |
| 2026-10-20 | Stop rule at the end of V6: the behavioural measurement is repeated through the real hook delivery with the trusted-sender instruction, N of at least 20 per cell for Codex and Claude Code; Codex must act on at least 80 percent of legitimate coordinator requests (observed rate and Wilson interval reported), harmful variants B, C, D, K, L and M stay at 0 acted; below 80 percent the Codex adapter is not built at V7 and the owner and controller revisit the plan. 80 percent is the owner's chosen threshold and N of 20 gives a wide interval | owner | accepted (section 14) |
| 2026-10-20 | Authorization (question 16) is a prerequisite of the Codex adapter at V7, not of G0; owned by the lane that writes the worker's brief, with the mailbox supplying the instruction text and trusted-sender list format; until then case B is not claimed to work | owner | accepted; the form of the trust key stays open. docs/platform/agent-mailbox/spec.md.sectionText:
## 18. Evidence and limits

- Measurements: one run per configuration on the owner's machine; screen-read timing resolution about 0.5 to 1 s; interactive tests ran inside tmux and, for agy, inside a temporary herdr workspace that was closed afterwards.
- The reference implementation (reason-network, commit 19b1fbf) was read, not run; its stop-hook claims were found to rest on output-shape tests only, and were then re-measured here.
- Not measured: cross-machine delivery, behaviour during compaction, many queued messages, two senders at once, a busy session with a human draft, the cost of the native hook kind in each CLI's real hook environment (a native verb through the shim measured about 10 ms), lock contention at real load, the human-input hook on Codex and agy, whether a runner-started Claude session can carry a scoped `accept`, and `codex queue` on a busy Codex session.
- The injection and loop evidence of sections 5.3 and 5.5 comes from print-mode and simulated runs (limits stated there), not from the real hook or extension delivery path.
- Council estimates (weeks per step, adapter breakage per quarter) are estimates, not observations.
- The council groups read the spec and probe reports and ran nothing.
- The second architecture panel (run `wf-run-1792502625986-9f47cb64`, commit `054129e97`) settled; its final packet and explanation live only on the machine that ran it (not in git) under `.fgos/assignments/unit-run-1792504271864-ec79d45e/` and `.fgos/assignments/unit-run-1792505792457-11102d7d/`. Its four residual red-team findings stayed open: the silence default for the 80 percent unit (closed here by the owner's per-cell answer), the A6 bundle of non-G0 cleanups, the A7 label, and a labelling defect in its source list.
- The first architecture panel's final report lives only on the machine that ran it (not in git) and was not closed by its workflow; this revision rests on the summary in `plans/reports/research-261020-1327-mailbox-spec-architecture-panel.md`. Unverified here: whether real models obey the peer frame, the cost of the native selector in a hook environment, the cost of a snapshot mutation, that a dying mutex holder releases the lock on the mailbox's own path, whether a peer-delivered prompt fires `UserPromptSubmit`, whether the registration side and the `send` side derive the same key from their environments, whether the host can serve one `hook` kind natively, a Rust resolver for the main checkout's `.fgos`, and the confinement reason `blind-confinement`.
- The V-REF-01 figures and the Event Store thresholds are quoted from `docs/platform/event-store/spec.md` and were not re-measured here.

# Reading Map (sản phẩm)

> **Quy tắc chuyển tiếp hiện hành:** bắt đầu ở `docs/reading-map.md` và `docs/platform/README.md`
> (hoặc tra cứu nhanh tại `docs/transitional-switchboard.md`), rồi dùng mapping current-source tường minh của
> portal area. Không suy authority từ path, ngày review, độ chi tiết, hoặc
> riêng metadata `Canonical:`. Bảng kiểm chứng Phase 00 sống tại
> `plans/260925-documentation-authority-unification/current-authority-map-2026-09-25.md`;
> bảng đó không promote, migrate hay retire source nào. Phase 00 và Phase 01 đã
> hoàn tất; Phase 02–09 vẫn chưa được authorize.

- `docs/platform-foundations.md` — văn bản gốc 10 luật nền platform (L1–L10); spec: docs/specs/platform-foundations.md
- `docs/backlog.md` — product backlog (PBI rows, scribing-owned)
- `docs/architecture-map.md` — bản chuẩn kiến trúc (v0.2, record ADR0010 (bản đồ kiến trúc là bản chuẩn)): 5 tầng + 2 lớp phủ, sổ component + sổ contract (CTR001–CTR009), nghi thức thẻ-căn-cước-trước-code
- `docs/work-item-lifecycle-vision.md` — tầm nhìn nền tảng: chu trình sống của work-item (mixed-autonomy, base-workflow + domain-extension); khung cho các PBI STR14-STR18
- `docs/platform/packaging-distribution/README.md` — portal hiện hành cho packaging/distribution: `fgctl` bootstrap/init/repair/upgrade, workspace activation, doctor/fix readiness, legacy Node compatibility, skill/instruction projections. Khi mục này mâu thuẫn với `docs/specs/distribution.md`, đọc portal + implementation-alignment trước; `docs/specs/distribution.md` hiện là legacy/generated-curated source trong lúc migration.
- `docs/distribution-vision.md` — tầm nhìn nền tảng lịch sử: cài đặt/setup/doctor ổn định + tái dùng được (không cần clone, global/project không xung đột — project ghi đè global, doctor/setup tự fix hạ tầng + merge config thiếu, module mới tự đăng ký năng lực config, CI như một phần của setup); đã được promote/supersede từng phần vào `docs/platform/packaging-distribution/vision.md`.
- `docs/specs/` — state layer: area spec + system-overview + bản đồ này
- `docs/routing-handoff-contract.md` — hợp đồng handoff agent↔agent + ranh giới tin cậy
- `docs/io-contract.md` — hợp đồng giao tiếp VÀO/RA của cửa CLI + bề mặt stdout `fgos-runner` (str46-io-contract): danh tính `writer`/`role`, envelope `fgos.v1` + ngoại lệ có lý do, exit-code một nguồn, sổ verb (`touchesState`/`externalEffect`/`paginated`/`multiValueFormat`), version token, ranh giới ngoài (STR38/STR48/STR83)
- `docs/coexistence.md` — doctrine chạy cạnh một harness agent khác (record ADR0009 (chống giao thoa lúc cài — fgOS khi cài không giao thoa tiến trình với harness khác)): lãnh địa, một-nhạc-trưởng-mỗi-phiên, nhường-nhịn lúc `init`, manifest `.fgos/coexistence.json`, Known Gaps chưa flip; `src/install/coexist.mjs` — cài đặt detection + manifest (read-only, không đè)
- `package.json` (`version`, `files`, `bin.fgos`, `bin.fgos-runner`) + `README.md` (mục `## Install`) — cài `fgos` VÀ `fgos-runner` từ ngoài source repo qua GitHub install, cả hai executable ngay sau cài; `test/install-packaging.test.mjs` — proof e2e (pack → install → chạy từ project ngoài, gồm cả hai binary); spec: docs/specs/distribution.md

Nguồn: `packages/agent-protocol/rust`
